item.title: Become a Grantmaker: The Fieldshaper Program
item.description:
Published on October 1, 2026 10:52 AM GMT

Summary

Over the course of a year, the Fieldshaper program develops you into a field-leading grantmaker. You’ll steward $1,000,000 in grant capital, receive a $125,000 annual stipend, and deploy that capital within a sub-field of one of three key areas (farmed animals, global health, or philanthropic infrastructure); building the track record to become a grantmaker who can shape a field.

Role Details

  • Title: Grantmaker-In-Residence (Leader of the X fund or Grantmaker in Y area also possible options)
  • Location: Hybrid: Remote with four mandatory in-person weeks (London; New York; San Francisco; a cause-track conference (London, Oxford or Mexico depending on cause area).
  • Compensation: A living stipend of ~$125,000 for the year
  • Duration: 12 months, full-time, February 2027 – January 2028
  • Focus areas: Farmed animal welfare, Philanthropic infrastructure, Global health, Global aid policy
  • Goal: To create the next generation of fieldshapers and active grantmakers
  • How to Apply: Visit elevatephilanthropy.com/fieldshaperprogram (Deadline: October 30)

Program

The Elevate Philanthropy fieldshaper program is a one-year training program that turns generalist, high-agency professionals into active grantmakers and general managers of problems. After 6 weeks of intensive training, each resident will deploy $1,000,000 of grant capital across the rest of the year, similar to a program officer role at a foundation or the leader of a philanthropic fund. The program aims to create a pathway into philanthropy and to develop the next generation of grantmakers, with an emphasis on active deployment and ecosystem thinking.

An active grantmaker sources and builds funding opportunities, rather than passively processing grant requests, and a fieldshaper owns an entire problem and aims to do whatever it takes to solve it. Developed by the co-founder of Ambitious Impact’s Charity Entrepreneurship program, an incubator behind 50+ high-impact charities, the program will train grantmakers who grow and affect the broader field they operate in.

Residents join one of three cause tracks (Animal Welfare, Global Health, or Philanthropic Infrastructure) and complete a six-week bootcamp before deploying capital into a specific sub-area within their chosen track (e.g. effective careers, or fish welfare in Asia). After this, five months of weekly structured sessions will run alongside live grantmaking. In the second half of the year, this tapers to weekly coaching as residents scale their deployment.

The program includes four in-person weeks: kick-off in London; one each at conferences in San Francisco and New York, and one at a cause-relevant conference (the AVA Summit or EAG London). These give fieldshapers time to get to know one another and to meet other grantmakers, funders, and actors in their field.

The year closes with a published piece of thought leadership, a one-year grant portfolio, and a demo-day-style event where residents present how they deployed their funding. Each pool is structured as a fund, with ongoing opportunities (though not guarantees) for top-ups and increased funding volume.

What you will do

  • The key goal is to deploy $1,000,000 in grant capital over the year impactfully.
  • Deploy this capital in a way that builds up the specific sub-field your granting is in, and in a way that is cost-effective in terms of the amount good done per $.
  • Deploy the majority of capital actively, e.g. creating opportunities or finding funding options that other grantmakers would miss.
  • Build a pipeline of ~20 funding opportunities in your cause track, run due diligence scaled to grant size, and make the case for or against funding to a review process.
  • Long-term, you will also consider assessing grant opportunities beyond single organizations; looking at fund managers and pooled vehicles, as well as actively co-building new projects in the field.
  • As you demonstrate your grantmaking ability, you will build out your portfolio and potentially fundraise with your new funder network, to further develop the area.

What you will learn

There is some basic learning about how to be a grantmaker (e.g. areas covered in this book), but the program is primarily focused on building active grantmaking and fieldshaping tools. This is broken down into 4 subsections:

  • Ecosystem-level thinking: For example, being able to analyze an area and determine where a marginal funder should deploy more capital to increase the total impact in the field.
  • Creating opportunities: For example, finding talented individuals and providing them with the necessary capital and support to advance an intervention in an area that would have not otherwise progressed.
  • Complex judgment: For example, being able to weigh off factors like the talent counterfactuals of a grant, and how a given project connects to the broader ecosystem.
  • Coordination: For example, if it makes sense to build up a donor collaboration in your area, and if so, which actors would be best positioned to join it.

What you leave with

A full year’s grantmaking track record, $1,000,000 deployed, a clear explanation for your theory of change for your field improving, published thought leadership under your name, introductions to grantmaking organisations, and working relationships with other highly talented fieldshapers you’ve learned and worked alongside.

We think anyone who goes through the program will be in a good place to be hired by existing and new foundations, launch their own fund, or kick off a career in active grantmaking in general. The reason we are running this program is that we believe there is a shortage of great grantmakers relative to funding and the hiring needs of growing foundations. Currently, there is no clear pathway for someone to get started into the field, and we see this long-term career impact as the primary driver of this program’s impact.

What we are looking for

Traits

  • Rigor and intellectual honesty under ambiguity; decision-making grounded in evidence.
  • Clear decision-making grounded in evidence and logic.
  • Comfort with the responsibility of directing large amounts of capital.
  • Ability to do high-quality self-directed work and gain knowledge quickly in a field.
  • No prior grantmaking experience required (we are equally excited about applicants who have none).

Example Target Demographics

Mid-career Professionals

Profile: Mid-career, currently in an adjacent sector (consulting, entrepreneurship, tech, policy) and looking for a structured route into philanthropy. This program appeals because it compresses the learning of years of on-the-job grantmaking into twelve months, backed by capital and warm introductions to grantmakers.

Concrete example: An ex-consultant who did three years of consulting and then founded her own firm. She is exceptional at the work and disappointed by its lack of impact. She has been filling evenings and weekends with volunteering and reading about social issues online. She has not picked a cause area and grantmaking feels like the best nonprofit role that would check boxes she has in terms of risk, intellectual challenge and impact at the same time. However, the path to get there is completely unclear.

Nonprofit Founders and Operators

Profile: People who have founded, run, or held senior operating roles at high-impact, evidence-based nonprofits and now want to move to the funding side. They arrive with grantee-side experience and a working knowledge of what organizations need from funders, which gives them an advantage in matching funders to the right grantees.

Example: A founder who spent seven years building an NGO. He wants more leverage than a single organisation can offer and has a deep sense of how the ecosystem he operates in works.

Philanthropic Actors without Fieldshaping Experience

Profile: People who have done grantmaking or philanthropic advisory before and are looking to increase their ability to do active grantmaking and more intentional fieldshaping.

Example: Someone who currently works at a classic foundation, but has found that even actors at the top of their field leave a lot of gaps in the ecosystem that are hard to fill, despite significant capital to deploy. They want their next grantmaking role to be more directly connected to building up the field.

Recruitment Process

The recruitment vetting is an intense process, but we aim to make each of the steps useful for the candidates in accessing their fit with grantmaking as a career path. Applications are open now, and close October 30th. We aim to have acceptance offers out to candidates by mid-December, with the program starting in February.

  1. Online application
  2. Online video screening
  3. Two interviews
  4. Two test tasks
  5. References

How to Apply: Visit elevatephilanthropy.com/fieldshaperprogram (Deadline: October 30)

item.title: GiveWell fundraising up 49% in 2025, driven overwhelmingly by 39 donors giving $1M+
item.description:
Published on October 2, 2026 9:19 PM GMT

Previously: GiveWell raised less than its 10th percentile forecast in 2023 · GiveWell fundraising up 17% in 2024

GiveWell has published its 2025 metrics, together with a metrics report and a public spreadsheet. As in previous years, I focus on how much was raised and who gave it. This year I also look at how concentrated GiveWell's donor base is.

Truth be told I kinda phoned it in on this one, the full Claude version with better charts is here

Summary

  • Returning donors gave $443.6M (up 77%). New donors gave $37.1M (up 112%), which is still below their 2020–2022 levels.
  • 39 donors giving $1M or more contributed $359.7M. That is 75% of identified donations through GiveWell and 90% of the year's increase. Every smaller size band also grew, by 13–27%.
  • The donor base is far more concentrated than an 80/20 rule. The top 20% of donors gave about 97% of the money, and about 0.26% of donors (roughly 90) gave 80%. Asking the question again within the top group (the top 20% of the top 20%, and so on) gives 94%, 93% and 92%, rather than 80% each time.

Returning donors drove the increase

Returning donors gave $443.6M, up 77% on 2024. That is 72% of all funds raised and 86% of the money from donors other than Coefficient Giving, both the highest shares in the series. The average returning donor gave about $20,800, against $12,300 in 2024.

New donors gave $37.1M, up 112%. This reverses three years of decline ($41.2M in 2022, $20.5M in 2023, $17.5M in 2024), but it remains below 2020–2022 levels. Anonymous giving fell 7% to $35.6M.

The number of donors rose for the first time since 2021. There were 13,796 new donors (up 34%) and 21,315 returning donors, a record. Together that makes 35,111 identified donors, up 14%, but still below the 2021 peak of about 41,900.

The increase was driven overwhelmingly by $1M+ donations

GiveWell reports donations that pass through its own accounts by donor size, with each donor placed in a band by their total gifts in the year. On this measure, identified donations rose by $230.4M, from $246.7M to $477.1M.

  • $1M+ donors: 39 (up from 26) gave $359.7M, up 138%. That accounts for $208.4M, or 90%, of the increase. The average gift in this band rose from $5.8M to $9.2M, so the growth came both from more very large donors and from larger gifts.
  • Every smaller band also grew: $100K–$1M by 27%, $10K–$100K by 23%, $1K–$10K by 19%, $100–$1K by 14% and under $100 by 13%. Giving below $1M rose 23% in total, against 10% in 2024, so growth was broader than last year even though the top band dominated it.
  • The $1M+ share of identified donations through GiveWell rose from 43% in 2020 to 61% in 2024 and 75% in 2025.

 

Is GiveWell's funding 80/20? No: it is far more concentrated

An 80/20 rule means the top 20% of donors give 80% of the money. If donations followed a Pareto distribution with that property, the pattern would repeat at every scale. The top 20% of the top 20% (4% of donors) would give 80% of that group's money, which is 64% of the total. The next level down (0.8% of donors) would give 51% of the total, and so on.

The size bands give exact figures only at their boundaries ($100, $1K, $10K, $100K and $1M). I interpolated between them (see the methodology section) and report ranges where the data leave room for doubt. For 2025:

  • The top 20% of donors (about 7,000) gave about 97% of the money (range 96.0–97.7%).
  • About 0.26% of donors, roughly 90 people or entities, gave 80% of the money (range 61–136 donors). In 2020–2024 the equivalent figure was 1.5–3.0% of donors.
  • The 39 donors giving $1M+, 0.11% of donors, gave 75%. This figure is exact.

Pareto within Pareto

Next, I asked the question again within each successive top group. At each level, what share of the group's money did the top 20% of that group give?

At every level the data can resolve, 2025 is well above 80%, and even the conservative end of each range is about 90%. Concentration has also risen over time. In 2020 the fourth level was almost exactly 80/20 (80.9%); in 2025 it was 91.5%. Beyond level 4 (about 11 donors, then about 2) the published bands cannot distinguish between very different distributions, so I do not report those levels.

Among the very largest donors, the distribution is close to a textbook 80/20. If the $1M+ band follows a Pareto tail, its average gift of $9.2M implies a tail index of α ≈ 1.12. An exact 80/20 rule corresponds to α ≈ 1.16. The largest donors are therefore slightly more concentrated than 80/20 among themselves. In earlier years α was about 1.19–1.28, slightly less concentrated than 80/20. The overall figure is so extreme because more than 30,000 donors give under $10K each, and together they account for under 7% of the money.

The figures above exclude Coefficient Giving. If its $100M is counted as a single additional donor, 80% of the combined money came from about 0.12% of donors (about 42). The nested shares rise to 98%, 95%, 94% and 93%.

Methodology and caveats

  • Data. The concentration analysis uses the spreadsheet's "Donations through GiveWell by Donor Size" tables, which give amounts and donor counts for identified donors. In 2025 these cover 35,098 donors and $477.1M. They exclude anonymous gifts ($18.9M through GiveWell), direct-to-charity gifts (for which no donor counts are published) and Coefficient Giving's $100M, which went directly to charities.
  • Interpolation. Within each band I assumed a truncated power-law distribution matched to the band's average gift. For the $1M+ band I assumed a Pareto tail with α = mean ÷ (mean − $1M). The ranges are the lowest and highest values consistent with the band counts and totals alone, with no distributional assumption.
  • What counts as a donor. The report does not say how foundations, donor-advised funds or effective-giving organisations are counted. If some $1M+ "donors" are intermediaries passing on many individuals' gifts, concentration among individuals is overstated. I would welcome clarification from GiveWell.
  • 2024 comparability. In the spreadsheet, 2024 donations through GiveWell ($255.8M) are about $8.2M more than non-Open Philanthropy giving minus direct-to-charity gifts. The 2024 size bands therefore appear to include about $8.2M of Open Philanthropy money, most likely in the $1M+ band. The 2025 bands include $39,625 from Coefficient Giving.
  • Metrics year. GiveWell's metrics year runs from 1 February to 31 January, so "2025" means 1 February 2025 to 31 January 2026.

Sources

  • GiveWell, GiveWell's 2025 Metrics and Impact (31 August 2026)
  • GiveWell, Metrics Report 2025 and Tables for the 2025 Metrics Report
  • GiveWell, Metrics Report 2024
  • GiveWell, How much funding does GiveWell expect to raise through 2025? (10 April 2023)
  • GiveWell, Coefficient Giving Commits $175 Million to GiveWell Opportunities (18 December 2025)
  • GiveWell, Scaling Our Impact, with Support from a $1 Billion Commitment (23 July 2026)

  • Every smaller band also grew: $100K–$1M by 27%, $10K–$100K by 23%, $1K–$10K by 19%, $100–$1K by 14% and under $100 by 13%. Giving below $1M rose 23% in total, against 10% in 2024, so growth was broader than last year even though the top band dominated it.
  • The $1M+ share of identified donations through GiveWell rose from 43% in 2020 to 61% in 2024 and 75% in 2025.

 

Is GiveWell's funding 80/20? No: it is far more concentrated

An 80/20 rule means the top 20% of donors give 80% of the money. If donations followed a Pareto distribution with that property, the pattern would repeat at every scale. The top 20% of the top 20% (4% of donors) would give 80% of that group's money, which is 64% of the total. The next level down (0.8% of donors) would give 51% of the total, and so on.

The size bands give exact figures only at their boundaries ($100, $1K, $10K, $100K and $1M). I interpolated between them (see the methodology section) and report ranges where the data leave room for doubt. For 2025:

  • The top 20% of donors (about 7,000) gave about 97% of the money (range 96.0–97.7%).

  • The 39 donors giving $1M+, 0.11% of donors, gave 75%. This figure is exact.

Next, I asked the question again within each successive top group. At each level, what share of the group's money did the top 20% of that group give?

At every level the data can resolve, 2025 is well above 80%, and even the conservative end of each range is about 90%. Concentration has also risen over time. In 2020 the fourth level was almost exactly 80/20 (80.9%); in 2025 it was 91.5%. Beyond level 4 (about 11 donors, then about 2) the published bands cannot distinguish between very different distributions, so I do not report those levels.

Among the very largest donors, the distribution is close to a textbook 80/20. If the $1M+ band follows a Pareto tail, its average gift of $9.2M implies a tail index of α ≈ 1.12. An exact 80/20 rule corresponds to α ≈ 1.16. The largest donors are therefore slightly more concentrated than 80/20 among themselves. In earlier years α was about 1.19–1.28, slightly less concentrated than 80/20. Methodology and caveats

  • Data. The concentration analysis uses the spreadsheet's "Donations through GiveWell by Donor Size" tables, which give amounts and donor counts for identified donors. They exclude anonymous gifts ($18.9M through GiveWell), direct-to-charity gifts (for which no donor counts are published) and Coefficient Giving's $100M, which went directly to charities.
  • Interpolation. Within each band I assumed a truncated power-law distribution matched to the band's average gift. For the $1M+ band I assumed a Pareto tail with α = mean ÷ (mean − $1M).   • What counts as a donor. The report does not say how foundations, donor-advised funds or effective-giving organisations are counted. If some $1M+ "donors" are intermediaries passing on many individuals' gifts, concentration among individuals is overstated. I would welcome clarification from GiveWell.
  • 2024 comparability. In the spreadsheet, 2024 donations through GiveWell ($255.8M) are about $8.2M more than non-Open Philanthropy giving minus direct-to-charity gifts. The 2024 size bands therefore appear to include about $8.2M of Open Philanthropy money, most likely in the $1M+ band. The 2025 bands include $39,625 from Coefficient Giving.
  • Metrics year. GiveWell's metrics year runs from 1 February to 31 January, so "2025" means 1 February 2025 to 31 January 2026.

item.description:
Published on October 5, 2026 2:30 PM GMT

A conflict of interest to flag: I'm the founder of Settled, a relationship and matchmaking company with free and paid tiers.  That may create bias in what I notice and what I recommend, so weigh these recommendations accordingly.  I’d love for some of you to sign up to Settled, but my aim here is to share something useful whether or not you ever do.
 

What this post is and isn’t 

  • We’re writing this because we hope it provide helpful insights - people have also asked, so here it is!
  • This post is based on:
    • Hundreds of hours of interviews and coaching  with 350+ singles
    • Data from Settled: nearly 2K completed questionnaires & hundreds of feedback forms from dates we set up
    • An ongoing literature review (with help from Claude) - 70+ papers reviewed
  • Our insights are observational, there's no control group and we collected all data for the purpose of setting up good dates, not research or analysis. We're including it because operational data from inside a matchmaking service is rare, not because it's complete or correct. 

Some observations and learnings from building Settled 

1. Dating apps are problematic; you should probably still use them

There are a variety of known problematic dynamics associated with dating apps, ie:

  • Apps waste a lot of time: we’ve talked to daters who spend tens of hours per week on the apps, and end up without quality dates
  • App use is associated with worse mental health: two 2026 meta-analyses (Cela & Wood 2026; Sharabi et al. 2026) find small-to-moderate associations with worse depression, anxiety, loneliness, and behavioural dysregulation. Although it's important to note that these studies are cross-sectional and compare users to non-users, which is confounded by the users being single.
  • Apps can increase unhelpful dating behavior: larger choice sets make daters more rejecting (acceptance falls ~27–29% across a session, Pronk & Denissen 2020), shift them onto cheap cues like height and weight (Lenton & Francesconi 2010), and produce less-satisfying, more reversible choices (D'Angelo & Toma 2017)
  • Apps are incentivized to keep you single and on the app as noted on a recent post from Clearer Thinking:

And despite this, dating apps are still a common way that couples meet today. 

A massive number of single people are on dating apps, so they're your biggest pool of potential matches. They are also good if you have broad preferences, or if a specialised app (ex. Feeld, Coffee Meets Bagel, ChristianMingle) narrows down your pool of preferences.  If it does make sense for you to keep using the apps, here’s some tips: 

  1. Use the apps alongside alternatives, ie: events, introductions through friends, communities you're in for their own sake, and matchmaking.
  2. Limit your use by limiting session frequency or length, and cap time when sending messages – just send it!
  3. Whilst Hinge and  Bumble tend to have the biggest pools, some apps that are built to avoid some of the dynamics listed above, two examples we know of:
    1. https://breeze.social/ (also has an EA aligned founder!) but worth noting it’s not in every region
    2. https://www.compassmeet.com/
  4. Move to meeting quickly. Finkel et al. found that extended pre-meeting communication builds expectations that the actual person then has to survive. A long text rapport is not evidence of anything.

2. Just ask questions and be on time.

People overthink first dates enormously. Whether the joke landed. Whether the outfit was wrong. Whether they should have picked somewhere else. If they should have offered to pay instead of split, or criticizing why they fell short of producing the single best insight on planet earth.

We ask both people for feedback after every date we set up, including what the other person could have done differently, and here’s what it tells us:

  • 54% of responses contained no improvement suggestion at all. The modal answer was some version of “no notes, they should just be themselves”

Among the responses that did suggest something, the most common themes we saw are:

  • ~20% Ask more questions, show curiosity, balance the conversational airtime (often mentioned by women as their biggest complaint)
  • ~11% Logistics: be on time, don’t end abruptly for because you take the date between engagements, etc

So, yeah: be yourself, ask questions, and be on time.

3. We’re bad at knowing how the first date went. 

If you've ever set two friends up and then spoken to both of them afterwards, you'll know how this goes: they describe two different evenings. That's not unusual, it's the normal case. Reading a stranger accurately, while also managing your own nerves and performance, is genuinely hard.

We see this phenomena at scale: we ask both daters for feedback after every date.  One question we ask is, “How interested did they seem in you?” on a 1-5 scale. Here’s how it pans out:

  • Of the people who thought the other person was interested in them (rated 4-5), that person was not open to seeing them again 25% of the time.
  • Of the people who thought the other person wasn't interested in them (rated 1-2), that person was open to seeing them again 73% of the time.
  • Of the people who were unsure if the other person was interested in them (rated 3), that person was open to seeing them again 56% of the time.

So yeah, it’s sometimes hard to tell how the first date went. 

And, we also learned that it’s hard to know how the date went even from your own perspective.  When asked if they want to see the person again for a second date, 30% of daters choose our “middle” option of “"not sure yet.”  Figuring out the answer to this question is one of the things we often work on together in coaching. 

Our advice:

  1. Overthinking afterwards is usually a bad use of your evening. Distraction techniques can be helpful. We often recommend worrying techniques like Worry Time and Practical vs. Hypothetical Worries.
  2. When in doubt, give it some more time to develop. If you’re not sure whether to go on a second date, we always suggest giving it a go. First and second (and even third dates!) are high-pressure, usually with a limited amount of time to get to know the person, so there’s a lot of noise and not much signal. Just collect more data; old habits and thought patterns can get in the way of genuinely great matches if you quit early. We’ve seen people not be sure about whether to give it a second date and then end up married with two kids to the same person!
  3. Signal clearly, don’t play it cool. If you want to see someone again, say it simply and clearly. We recommend doing this after the date. It’s more about solving for confusion than a wildly romantic gesture. We’ve seen many potential relationships die because of lack of communication and both people guessing what the other thinks.
  4. Don’t expect it to be obvious to you how the date went. Debriefing with friends can be great, and journaling can soothe an active mind, but watch out for finding yourself in a bit of an echo chamber, and remember that people bring their own experiences, biases and frames into how they give advice, which is often very unreliable. Coaching, journaling, or talking to trusted friends can be good ways to think through this. 

4. Physical attraction is just one ingredient amongst many 

The topic of physical attractiveness comes up often and in many different ways in dating. We don’t want to undercut its importance: research shows that physical attraction is not a minor factor (Eastwick et al. 2014), and there are real population-level patterns in what people find attractive.

But mostly, we talk to people who care about physical attraction amongst many other things, have a rough ‘type’ that’s somewhat flexible, and are generally more worried about things like kindness, intelligence, and open mindedness.  A few items we think are worth mentioning:

All of the dates we’ve set up are blind dates, meaning neither person sees a photo of the person before the date. So, there are 100s of smart, kind EAs who are happy to go on dates without seeing the other person in advance.  

Here’s what 1K+ singles from the Settled community reported when we asked, "How important are looks when it comes to who you're attracted to?" As you can see below, 12% ranked it as very important, but also 13% say they have no type or that looks don't matter. Many say attraction builds once they know someone.

Note that this group is people who have self selected into dating via our service which does blind dates and are mostly EA/Rationalist, so we expect these numbers reflect those factors.

 

 

 

OkCupid “blind-date day” saw that blinding dates made almost no difference in whether people enjoyed the date. 
In 2013 OkCupid ran a blind-date app, Crazy Blind Date, that paired about 10,000 people for in-person dates. Each person saw only a first name and a scrambled photo of the other. Afterwards, the app asked both people how the date went. When OkCupid matched those answers against the daters' attractiveness scores, the gap in looks between the two people made almost no difference to whether they enjoyed the date. About 75% of women and 85% of men had a good time. 
 

Rudder's summary: people "appear to be heavily preselecting online for something that, once they sit down in person, doesn't seem important to them." 
 

Note: this is company data reported in a book, not a peer-reviewed study.

5. Dating doesn’t have to suck. 

When people tell us dating is miserable, they're usually describing a fairly specific set of things:

  • Being ghosted, or having your time wasted (usually repeatedly)
  • The hours spent on swiping, profiles, and texting that amount to nothing
  • The uncertainty of having no idea why you're not getting first or second dates.
  • And then concluding there's something badly wrong with you, losing hope, or feeling terrible about it.

Notice that most of these are not about the dates themselves. Most of the misery is in the overhead and the silence.

We think dating sucks less when a few conditions are true, and these are the conditions we try to create at Settled:

  • Dates are set up for you, without all the faff
  • You’re dating within a curated, screened pool of people who are intellectually curious and deeply kind
  • You’re dating others with the same community affiliations (and we try to take into account sensitivities related to work in our matchmaking)
  • You have someone in your court to debrief with before and after dates
  • We help you break out of negative patterns, identify limiting beliefs and improve your confidence
  • You get feedback on how you’re showing up and how it's being interpreted 

Now, do these conditions mean that we will definitely find your person? We don't know, and per 70+ paper reviews, nobody knows. 

But here’s our evidence that dating doesn’t have to suck: 85% of the time, daters say their Settled date was a good use of time. 78% said that they’re open to seeing their first date again and 72% end up in a serious relationship within 6 months.

If this resonates with you, join us

We hope this write up was helpful.  

 

If this thinking resonated with you and interested in trying a different approach to dating, you can:

  • Sign up to join Settled’s database here
  • Follow us on X - we post anonymous profiles of EA singles, so you can browse for yourself or for a friend :)
  • Come see us at an upcoming EAG singles events
  • Reach out to me at ann@settledlove.com

 

A few things to know that may be unusual about how we work:

  • Dates are blind dates, meaning they are set up without photos in advance
  • Feedback after every date is mandatory. It’s how we improve at the individual and aggregate level.
  • We have free and paid offerings
  • We started in London, but have expanded across the EU and to hubs in the US including San Francisco, New York, and Washington DC - sign up to our EAG mixer NYC or Berlin
  • Our database is gender balanced.
